content: Immunization rates for both children and adults have been increasing, but they still fall short of optimal levels. Consequently, vaccine-preventable diseases continue to occur. The growing complexity of immunization schedules, coupled with the increasing demands on primary care providers, underscores the importance of identifying and implementing effective strategies to enhance immunization coverage in primary care settings. A significant challenge in many immunization programs worldwide is adopting a population-based approach to identify all eligible individuals, such as children requiring the measles vaccine. However, this challenge is being mitigated by the use of immunization registries and electronic health records. Another critical issue is determining the most effective strategies to achieve high vaccination rates. These strategies can be categorized into three main types: (1) patient-oriented interventions, such as reminders or recalls directed at patients; (2) provider-focused interventions; and (3) system-level interventions, such as school immunization laws. Among these, patient reminder and recall systems are one of the most extensively studied and widely implemented approaches. The objective of this review was to assess and compare the effectiveness of various patient reminder and recall interventions in improving immunization uptake. The review included randomized trials, controlled before-and-after studies, and interrupted time series that evaluated patient reminder or recall interventions aimed at increasing immunization rates in children, adolescents, and adults across various settings. Studies involving hospitalized patients or those focusing on travel-specific immunizations were excluded. The analysis adhered to the rigorous methodological standards of the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) Group. The review included 75 studies conducted in 10 countries, involving a total of 138,625 participants across outpatient, community-based, and primary care settings. Patient reminder and recall interventions, such as telephone calls, autodialer messages, letters, postcards, text messages, or combinations of these methods, were found to likely improve immunization rates. The pooled analysis of 55 studies demonstrated a risk ratio (RR) of 1.28 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.23 to 1.35), with a risk difference of 8%, based on moderate-certainty evidence. Specific single-method reminders were shown to be effective. Postcards improved immunization rates with a risk ratio of 1.18 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.30) based on eight studies involving 27,734 participants. Text messages were associated with a risk ratio of 1.29 (95% CI 1.15 to 1.44) from six studies with 7,772 participants. Autodialer messages showed a risk ratio of 1.17 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.32) based on five studies with 11,947 participants. Telephone calls likely improved immunization rates, with a risk ratio of 1.75 (95% CI 1.20 to 2.54) from seven studies involving 9,120 participants. Letters to patients also likely improved immunization rates, with a risk ratio of 1.29 (95% CI 1.21 to 1.38) based on 27 studies involving 81,100 participants. High-certainty evidence indicated that reminders improved immunization rates for childhood vaccinations (RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.29; risk difference of 8%) and adolescent vaccinations (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.42; risk difference of 7%). Moderate-certainty evidence suggested that reminders likely improved childhood influenza vaccination rates (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.99; risk difference of 22%) and adult influenza vaccination rates (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.43; risk difference of 9%). For adult pneumococcal, tetanus, hepatitis B, and other non-influenza vaccinations, reminders may improve immunization rates, but the evidence is of low certainty, and the confidence interval includes the possibility of no effect (RR 2.08, 95% CI 0.91 to 4.78). In conclusion, patient reminder and recall systems implemented in primary care settings are likely to be effective in increasing the proportion of individuals who receive immunizations. These interventions represent a valuable strategy for improving vaccination coverage and reducing the burden of vaccine-preventable diseases.
